title: Text embeddings and semantic search
summary: How a transformer becomes a sentence embedding model and how real ones are trained, then how to search with it: chunking, vector size, adaptation, hybrid fusion, re-ranking, ColBERT and SPLADE.

lessons.title: Why keyword match misses meaning and cross-encoders are too slow

blocks.md:
From the prerequisite course you know an **embedding**: a learned map from an item to a vector, trained so that related items land close together. This course applies that idea to whole sentences and passages, and uses it to search. First, the problem it solves.

**Lexical search** such as BM25 scores a document only by the query words it contains.

BM25 (BM stands for best matching; it was built for the Okapi search system and first published in 1994) gives each query word that appears in a document a score, and adds them up. A word's score grows with how often it appears in the document, with diminishing returns, and is multiplied by its **inverse document frequency** (IDF): roughly the log of the number of documents divided by the number that contain the word. A word found in almost every document gets an IDF near 0; a word found in only a few gets a large one, so rare words decide the ranking.

That is fast and precise, but it is blind to meaning: two texts that say the same thing with different words share no terms and get no credit.

blocks.prompt: The DPR paper (Dense Passage Retrieval, 2020) gives this example. Query: *Who is the bad guy in lord of the rings?* Passage: *Sala Baker is best known for portraying the villain Sauron in the Lord of the Rings trilogy.* Which query words can a keyword matcher use to find this passage?
blocks.reveal: Only *lord* and *rings* (plus stopwords like *the* and *of*, which carry almost no weight). The words that carry the question, *bad guy*, never appear: the passage says *villain*. Any page about Lord of the Rings film locations matches just as well. A **dense** retriever turns each text into a short vector of a few hundred numbers, all of them in use; a keyword view is **sparse**, with one slot per vocabulary word and almost all of them zero. A dense retriever can learn that *bad guy* and *villain* mean the same thing and place them close together.

blocks.md: One fix is a **cross-encoder**: feed the query and the passage together into a transformer such as BERT and have it output one relevance score. A **transformer** is a neural network that splits text into **tokens** (words or pieces of words) and keeps one vector per token. Its core operation is **attention**: in each layer, every token's vector is replaced by a weighted average of all the tokens' vectors, with weights that grow with how well each pair matches. **BERT** (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers, Google, 2018) is a transformer pretrained to fill in hidden words from the words on both sides, hence bidirectional.

Because attention runs across both texts, every query token can look directly at every passage token, so a cross-encoder is accurate. The catch is cost: every (query, passage) pair needs its own full forward pass, and nothing can be computed ahead of time.

The Sentence-BERT paper (SBERT; Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) quantifies this. Finding the most similar pair among 10,000 sentences means scoring every pair. Each of the $n$ sentences pairs with the $n-1$ others, which counts every pair twice (A with B, then B with A), so divide by 2:

blocks.caption: About 50 million BERT inferences, which the SBERT paper reports as roughly 65 hours.

blocks.md: The alternative is a **bi-encoder** (SBERT calls it a **siamese network**: the same encoder, with the same weights, applied to each input separately, like identical twins): one encoder turns each text into a vector **on its own**, and relevance is a cheap vector similarity such as cosine. Each of the 10,000 sentences is encoded once (about 5 seconds in the SBERT paper), and all pairwise cosines then take about 0.01 seconds. For search, the passage vectors are computed once, offline, and reused for every query.

blocks.title: Cross-encoder versus bi-encoder

scenes.caption: Cross-encoder: query and passage enter the model together, so attention compares every query token with every passage token. Accurate, but there is nothing to reuse between pairs.
Scoring a new passage against the same query means a full forward pass again. For N passages, that is N passes per query.
Bi-encoder: each text is encoded separately by the same network into a fixed-length vector. Relevance is just a cosine between two vectors.
The passage vector never depends on the query, so it is computed once offline and stored. At query time only the short query is encoded.

blocks.title: Model calls to find the closest pair among n texts

scenes.caption: Both axes are logarithmic. The cross-encoder grows quadratically, the bi-encoder linearly. At 10,000 texts the gap is about 5,000x in forward passes; the cosines left over for the bi-encoder are cheap arithmetic.

blocks.md: A bi-encoder trades accuracy for speed in one specific way: the passage vector cannot look at the query. In exchange, every passage is encoded once, ahead of time, and search becomes a nearest-neighbor lookup among vectors. Everything else in this course follows from that trade.

Misconception: *semantic search understands meaning*. It finds vectors that are geometrically close, and closeness means whatever the training pairs rewarded. A model trained on question-answer pairs puts a question near its answer, not necessarily near a paraphrase of the question.

blocks.question: You must rank 1,000,000 passages for each incoming query. Which cost profile describes a pure cross-encoder versus a bi-encoder at query time?
options: Both need 1,000,000 forward passes per query; the bi-encoder just uses a smaller model
Cross-encoder: 1,000,000 forward passes per query. Bi-encoder: 1 forward pass for the query plus 1,000,000 vector similarities
Cross-encoder: 1 forward pass per query. Bi-encoder: 1,000,000 forward passes
Both need 1 forward pass, because attention handles all passages at once
blocks.explain: The cross-encoder has to read the query together with every passage, so its work scales with the corpus on every query. The bi-encoder encoded the passages offline; online it encodes only the query and then does cheap dot products, which an index can speed up further.

blocks.question: Which property is what makes the bi-encoder's precomputation possible?
options: Its passage vector is a function of the passage alone
It uses cosine instead of dot product
It is a smaller model than a cross-encoder
It tokenizes the query and passage with the same vocabulary
blocks.explain: Precomputation needs the passage representation to be independent of the query. Cosine versus dot product, model size and vocabulary are all irrelevant to that; a cross-encoder can share vocabulary and still cannot precompute anything.

lessons.title: From token vectors to one sentence vector: pooling and cosine

blocks.md:
A transformer encoder such as BERT reads a text and outputs **one vector per token** (BERT's tokenizer, WordPiece, splits text into words and pieces of words from a fixed vocabulary of about 30,000; a text's length limit is counted in these word pieces), each already mixed with context from the other tokens. Search needs **one vector per text**, of a fixed length regardless of how long the text is. The step that collapses token vectors into one is called **pooling**.

Sentence-BERT tried three options: take the output at the `[CLS]` position (BERT puts this special token at the start of every input; the name is short for classification, because its pretraining used that position's output to classify the input as a whole), take the mean of all token vectors (MEAN), or take the per-dimension max (MAX). Its default is MEAN.

The widely used all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model also uses mean pooling. Its name reads in parts: MiniLM is a family of small transformers that Microsoft trained to imitate a larger one, L6 means 6 layers, and all means the sentence-transformers team fine-tuned it on all their training data, more than 1 billion text pairs. It outputs 384 numbers per text.

There is one trap. Texts are processed in batches, and a batch must be rectangular, so short texts are padded with `[PAD]` tokens. The encoder still produces output vectors at padding positions, and they are not zero. The **attention mask** (1 for real tokens, 0 for padding) tells pooling which rows to average.

Toy example (simplified to 4 dimensions; real models use 384 or 768): the text *cheap flights* becomes `[CLS] cheap flights [SEP]` (`[SEP]` is BERT's separator token, which closes each text segment), padded with two `[PAD]` tokens to match a longer neighbor in the batch.

blocks.title: Token output vectors for cheap flights, padded to 6

scenes.caption: The encoder outputs a 4-number vector for each of the 6 positions, including the two padding positions. Their values are made up for this toy example.
The attention mask is 1 for the four real tokens and 0 for padding. Masked mean pooling averages only the highlighted rows.
Forgetting the mask averages all six rows, so the padding vectors pull the result toward [-0.5, -0.2, 0.6, 0.5].

blocks.title: Pooling, then normalizing to unit length

scenes.caption: Masked mean: sum the four real rows and divide by 4.
Divide by the length 0.566 to get a unit vector. This is the sentence embedding; its length is now 1.
Without the mask: sum all six rows and divide by 6. Padding drags every dimension.
Normalized, the unmasked vector has cosine 0.682 with the correct one. Same sentence, different vector, only because of what else was in the batch.

blocks.code:
import torch.nn.functional as F

def mean_pool(token_embeddings, attention_mask):
    # token_embeddings: (batch, seq_len, dim); attention_mask: (batch, seq_len)
    mask = attention_mask.unsqueeze(-1).float()
    summed = (token_embeddings * mask).sum(dim=1)
    counts = mask.sum(dim=1).clamp(min=1e-9)
    return summed / counts

emb = mean_pool(outputs.last_hidden_state, batch["attention_mask"])
emb = F.normalize(emb, p=2, dim=1)  # unit length: dot product == cosine
blocks.caption: Masked mean pooling then L2 normalization, the same steps shown on the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model card.

blocks.md: To compare two embeddings, the standard measure is **cosine similarity**: the dot product divided by both lengths, so only the direction counts. It ranges from -1 to 1. If both vectors are already unit length, cosine and dot product are the same number, which is why systems normalize once at indexing time and then use the cheaper dot product.

blocks.prompt: Query $q=(1,0)$. Document $a=(0.8,0.6)$ has length 1. Document $b=(3,4)$ has length 5. Which one ranks first by dot product, and which by cosine?
blocks.reveal: Dot product: $q\cdot a = 0.8$, $q\cdot b = 3$, so **b** wins. Cosine: $0.8/1 = 0.8$ for a and $3/5 = 0.6$ for b, so **a** wins. Dot product rewards length; cosine ignores it. Neither is wrong: use the one the model was trained with. DPR, for example, trained with dot product, while SBERT used cosine.

blocks.md:
Does any pretrained transformer give good sentence embeddings if you just mean-pool it? The SBERT paper tested this on semantic textual similarity (STS) benchmarks: sentence pairs that human annotators scored for how close their meanings are (for example from 0 to 5). The test asks how well the cosine between the two sentence vectors ranks the pairs the way the annotators did.

The measure is **Spearman rank correlation**: replace each list of scores by ranks (1 for the highest, 2 for the next, and so on), then compute the ordinary correlation between the two rank lists. It is 1 when the two orders agree exactly, near 0 when they are unrelated and -1 when one is the reverse of the other. Because it uses only the order, the scale of cosine does not matter. The paper reports it times 100.

The fine-tuned model in the figure was trained on **natural language inference** (NLI) data: sentence pairs labeled entailment (the second follows from the first), contradiction or neutral. SBERT used SNLI (570,000 pairs) and MultiNLI (430,000 pairs). The name SBERT-NLI-base means SBERT trained on NLI, starting from BERT-base, the 12-layer BERT whose vectors have 768 numbers.

blocks.title: Average STS Spearman correlation (SBERT paper, Table 1)

scenes.caption: Off-the-shelf BERT, unfine-tuned: averaging its token vectors scores 54.81 and the [CLS] vector 29.19, both worse than simply averaging GloVe word vectors (61.32).
The same BERT, fine-tuned as a siamese bi-encoder on sentence pairs (SBERT-NLI-base), reaches 74.89, above the earlier dedicated sentence encoders.

blocks.prompt: Why does a pooled pretrained model do so badly on STS? Embed six sentences: two paraphrases about a guitar and four unrelated ones (stocks, penguins, a router, a recipe). Mean-pool the raw pretrained MiniLM, before any sentence training. Guess the average cosine between unrelated pairs.
blocks.reveal: About **0.83**, measured on this Mac. The paraphrase pair scores 0.92, barely above it, so cosine says almost nothing about meaning. The vectors are **anisotropic**: they occupy a narrow cone instead of spreading in all directions, a property Ethayarajh (2019) measured in almost every layer of BERT, ELMo and GPT-2. After contrastive training of that same checkpoint (it is the starting point of all-MiniLM-L6-v2, per its model card) the unrelated pairs average -0.002 and the paraphrase scores 0.68: the cone has opened up.

blocks.title: Mean-pooled cosines, before and after contrastive training

scenes.caption: Raw pretrained MiniLM, masked mean pooling: unrelated pairs average 0.83, the paraphrase 0.92. Everything looks similar to everything.
BERT-base is less extreme but still crowded: unrelated 0.50, paraphrase 0.86.

After contrastive training on sentence pairs (all-MiniLM-L6-v2): unrelated pairs fall to -0.002 on average while the paraphrase keeps 0.68. Now the gap carries meaning. Six sentences only, so read it as an illustration.

blocks.md: Pooling a pretrained language model does not give you a good embedding model. BERT was never trained to make cosine meaningful; the training objective in the next lesson is what does that.

blocks.question: Your service embeds documents in batches of 32. The same document gets clearly different vectors depending on which batch it lands in. What is the most likely bug?
options: The model is non-deterministic because of dropout at inference
Cosine similarity is unstable for vectors of length 1
Mean pooling is averaging over padding positions instead of using the attention mask
The tokenizer lowercases differently per batch
blocks.explain: Padding length depends on the longest text in the batch, so if pooling ignores the attention mask, the number and effect of [PAD] rows changes with batch composition. Dropout is disabled in eval mode, and tokenization does not depend on the batch.

blocks.question: Your vectors are L2-normalized at indexing time and queries are normalized too. A teammate switches the scoring function from cosine to dot product to save time. What happens to the ranking?
options: It is identical, because for unit vectors the dot product equals the cosine
It changes, because dot product favors longer documents
It reverses
It becomes random
blocks.explain: Cosine divides the dot product by the two lengths. When both lengths are 1, that division does nothing, so the scores and the ranking are identical. This is exactly why normalizing once is standard practice.

blocks.md:
To make cosine meaningful, train on **pairs** that should be close: a question and the passage that answers it, a title and its abstract, two paraphrases. The training signal is a ranking: query $q_i$ should be closer to its own passage $p_i$ than to other passages.

Where do the other passages come from? The DPR paper uses a cheap trick called **in-batch negatives**. Take a batch of $B$ pairs, encode the $B$ queries and $B$ passages, and compute all $B \times B$ similarities $S = QP^\top$. Here the rows of $Q$ are the query vectors and the rows of $P$ are the passage vectors, so entry $S_{ij}$ of the product is the similarity of query $i$ with passage $j$. The diagonal entries are the correct pairs; every off-diagonal entry is a free negative. Each query gets $B-1$ negatives without encoding anything extra.

blocks.caption: For each query i, a softmax over its row of scaled similarities gives the probability of its own passage i; the loss is minus the log of that probability, averaged over the B rows. s is the scale (1 / temperature).

blocks.md:
This is the same loss known as InfoNCE, from the contrastive predictive coding paper (van den Oord and others, 2018), where NCE stands for noise-contrastive estimation: learning by telling the true example apart from noise samples, here the other passages in the batch. In the sentence-transformers library (the Python library released by the SBERT authors) it is `MultipleNegativesRankingLoss`, which uses cosine similarity with a default **scale** $s = 20$, equivalent to a temperature of 0.05. The scaled similarities $s \cdot S_{ij}$ are the **logits** of the softmax: the raw scores it turns into probabilities. The loss's docstring notes values between 10 and 100 are common, and that with dot product you would set the scale to 1.

Worked example, $B = 4$ (numbers are a made-up snapshot early in training):

blocks.title: In-batch similarities, then row softmax at scale 20

scenes.caption: Cosine similarities between 4 queries and the 4 passages in the batch. The diagonal holds the true pairs; the 12 off-diagonal cells are free negatives.
Each row goes through softmax(20 x cosine). Row q1 puts 0.98 on its own passage. Losses per row are -ln of the diagonal: 0.019, 0.226, 0.027, 0.160, mean 0.108.
Row q2 is the hard case: p3 has cosine 0.48, close to the true 0.55, so p3 still gets 0.20 of the probability. Most of the gradient in this batch comes from here and from q4 vs p1.

blocks.prompt: Keep row q2 (cosines 0.30, 0.55, 0.48, 0.12) but use scale 1 instead of 20. What probability does the softmax give the correct passage p2?
blocks.reveal: Only **0.30**, against 0.28 for p3. Cosines live in [-1, 1], so differences of 0.07 barely move a softmax at scale 1, and the loss stays above 1.1 for every row (1.212 here; the maximum, a uniform guess, is $\ln 4 = 1.386$). Scaling by 20 turns the 0.07 gap into a logit gap of 1.4, giving 0.80 vs 0.20. The scale sets how sharply the model is pushed to separate positives from near misses.

blocks.title: Row q2 softmax: scale 1 versus scale 20

scenes.caption: Scale 1: the distribution is almost flat, since the logits are the raw cosines 0.30, 0.55, 0.48, 0.12.
Scale 20: the same cosines become logits 6, 11, 9.6 and 2.4. The true passage gets 0.80; the hard negative keeps 0.20; the easy ones are near 0.

blocks.md:
Why does this matter for which negatives you use? The gradient of softmax cross-entropy with respect to a negative's logit is that negative's probability $p_j$. Here is why. Write row $i$'s logits as $z_j$. The loss is $-z_i + \ln \sum_k e^{z_k}$. The derivative of the log-sum with respect to $z_j$ is $e^{z_j} / \sum_k e^{z_k}$, which is exactly the softmax probability $p_j$. The $-z_i$ term only touches the true passage, whose gradient is therefore $p_i - 1$. For every negative it is just $p_j$.

An **easy negative** with $p_j \approx 0$ teaches almost nothing. A **hard negative**, one that looks relevant but is not, carries most of the signal.

DPR therefore added one **BM25 hard negative** per question: a passage that scores high for the question's keywords but does not contain the answer. Each such passage is shared as a negative by every question in the batch.

The figure is DPR's ablation, an experiment that changes one ingredient at a time. It uses Natural Questions (NQ): real Google search queries, with answers that annotators marked in Wikipedia articles. The score is **top-20 retrieval accuracy** on the dev set (the held-out split used for tuning): the share of questions for which at least one of the 20 retrieved passages contains the answer. **Gold** negatives are the positive passages that belong to other questions.

blocks.title: DPR ablation: top-20 retrieval accuracy (NQ dev, Table 3)

scenes.caption: Same 7 gold negatives per question, but taken from the current batch instead of sampled from the whole training set: 63.1 to 69.1. In-batch reuse adds many more training pairs for free.
Bigger batches mean more negatives per query (7, 31, 127): 69.1, 70.8, 73.0. Accuracy rises steadily with batch size.
Adding one BM25 hard negative per question at batch 128 jumps to 78.0. DPR reports that a second BM25 negative did not help further.

blocks.md: In-batch negatives assume the other passages are wrong. If the batch holds two copies of the same passage, or two paraphrased questions, the loss pushes a correct answer away. sentence-transformers recommends the `NO_DUPLICATES` batch sampler, which never puts the same text twice in one batch, for this reason. Hard negatives mined automatically can also be unlabeled positives, so they need filtering; the lesson on modern training recipes shows how.

Contrastive training with in-batch negatives is what turns a language model into an embedding model: pull each true pair together, push everything else in the batch apart, with a scale (temperature) that controls how sharply.

blocks.question: DPR trains with batch size 128 and one BM25 negative per question, shared across the batch. How many negative passages does each question see?
blocks.explain: 127 in-batch gold passages from the other questions, plus all 128 BM25 negatives in the batch (each question's BM25 negative is shared with everyone). DPR's table lists this configuration as 127+128.

blocks.question: After some training, every off-diagonal cosine in a batch is below 0.1 while every diagonal is above 0.8. The loss is near zero, but retrieval on real queries is still mediocre. What is the most useful change?
options: Lower the scale to 1 so the loss becomes larger
Remove normalization so vectors can grow
Add hard negatives such as BM25 results that do not contain the answer
Shrink the batch so each step is faster
blocks.explain: Random in-batch negatives have become too easy, so their gradient ($p_j$) is near zero. Hard negatives restore signal on exactly the near misses the model gets wrong at search time. Lowering the scale only flattens the softmax, and a smaller batch gives fewer negatives.

lessons.title: Lab: train a tiny encoder with in-batch negatives and measure it

blocks.md:
Reading the loss is one thing; watching it work is another. In this lab you train an encoder from random weights, on a laptop CPU, in about ten seconds per run (our runs took 8 to 12 seconds on 2 threads, depending on what else the machine was doing), and then measure it the way retrieval systems are measured.

The data is the [natural-questions pairs](https://huggingface.co/datasets/sentence-transformers/natural-questions) set: about 100,000 (Google search query, Wikipedia passage) pairs. Hold out 5,000 pairs. Their 5,000 passages become the corpus, and 1,000 of their queries become test queries, so each test query has one relevant passage among 5,000. The other 95,231 pairs are for training. NQ questions often share a passage, so 382 of the 1,000 test passages also appear in training pairs with other questions: the lab tests new questions, not unseen passages.

The encoder is deliberately tiny: a **bag of word pieces**. Text is split with the WordPiece tokenizer of all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (the vocabulary only, none of its weights). Each word piece looks up a row of 128 numbers in a trainable table, the rows are averaged, and the average is normalized to length 1. There is no attention, so word order is ignored. The table holds 30,522 x 128, about 3.9 million numbers, and it starts random.

Training uses exactly the loss from the previous lesson: a batch of 256 pairs, the 256 x 256 cosine matrix times scale 20, and cross-entropy with the diagonal as the target.

blocks.code:
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
torch.set_num_threads(2)

class Tiny(nn.Module):                      # bag of word pieces
    def __init__(self, vocab=30522, dim=128):
        super().__init__()
        self.emb = nn.EmbeddingBag(vocab, dim, mode="mean")
    def forward(self, flat_ids, offsets):    # all token ids, start of each text
        return F.normalize(self.emb(flat_ids, offsets), dim=-1)

def in_batch_loss(q, p, scale=20.0, group=None):
    logits = scale * q @ p.T                 # (B, B) scaled cosines
    B = len(q)
    if group:                                # each query only sees its group
        gid = torch.arange(B) // group
        logits = logits.masked_fill(gid[:, None] != gid[None, :], float("-inf"))
    return F.cross_entropy(logits, torch.arange(B))  # target: the diagonal

# per step: q = model(*batch_queries); p = model(*batch_passages)
# loss = in_batch_loss(q, p); opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
blocks.caption: The core of the lab script (Adam, learning rate 0.005, batch 256, 3 epochs). The group option masks out part of the batch so you can change how many negatives each query sees without changing anything else.

blocks.md:
Two numbers summarize a ranking. **Recall@k** is the share of a query's relevant passages that appear in its top $k$, averaged over queries. With one relevant passage per query, it is the share of queries whose passage made the top $k$.

**nDCG@10** (normalized discounted cumulative gain) also rewards *where* the hit lands. A relevant result at rank $r$ earns $1/\log_2(r+1)$: 1 at rank 1, 0.63 at rank 2, 0.5 at rank 3. Sum that over the top 10 and divide by the best possible sum, so a perfect ranking scores 1. It is the main metric of the BEIR and MTEB retrieval benchmarks. The search evaluation courses (*Search evaluation basics*, *Ranking metrics*) treat both in depth.

blocks.tex: \mathrm{nDCG@10} = \frac{\sum_{r=1}^{10} \mathrm{rel}_r / \log_2(r+1)}{\text{the same sum for the ideal ranking}}
blocks.caption: rel_r is 1 if the result at rank r is relevant, else 0. With a single relevant passage, nDCG@10 is 1/log2(rank+1) when the passage is in the top 10, and 0 otherwise.

blocks.prompt: Before any training the table is random. Picking 10 passages out of 5,000 at random would give recall@10 of 0.2%. Does the untrained encoder do that badly?
blocks.reveal: No: it measured **27.5%**. Averaging random vectors still works as a random projection of the bag of words, so a query and a passage that share word pieces share some of the same random rows and point in similar directions: crude word overlap for free. Training is what adds meaning. After 3 epochs (1113 steps, about 9 seconds on 2 CPU threads) the same model reaches 85.6% recall@10 and nDCG@10 0.723.

blocks.title: Recall@10 vs negatives per query (batch 256, same steps)

scenes.caption: Each query sees only 1 other passage in its group: recall@10 65.2%. The data, steps and model are identical in every bar; only the masked part of the batch changes.
7 and 31 negatives: 75.3% and 80.9%. More negatives per query give a harder ranking task in every step.
The full batch, 255 negatives: 85.6%. Same direction as DPR's batch-size ablation, measured here with a 4-million-number toy model.

blocks.md:
These are single runs with seed 0, but the ordering is not luck: rerunning 31 and 255 negatives and scale 1 with seeds 1 and 2 moved recall@10 by at most 1 point. Two more runs from the same script. With scale 1 instead of 20 (same 255 negatives), recall@10 falls to 75.0% and nDCG@10 to 0.615, against 0.723: the flat softmax from the previous lesson barely separates near misses.

And the baseline: BM25 on the same 5,000 passages scores recall@10 91.5% and nDCG@10 0.802. Exact matching is strong on this set, where questions and their passages often share names and other rare words, and the toy model has no word order and saw each pair only 3 times. A pretrained transformer encoder is what closes that gap.
Always run BM25 on the same queries before you celebrate a dense model. A trained encoder that loses to a 1994 formula on your data is common, and you only find out by measuring both.

The lab runs on a CPU because the model is a lookup table. The same loop with a transformer encoder is what the sentence-transformers trainer runs; the adaptation lesson later uses it to fine-tune a real model on a laptop.

blocks.question: In the lab, each query in a batch of 256 can be limited to a group of 8 passages instead of all 256. Which statement about that experiment is right?
options: The group-of-8 run sees fewer training pairs, so it is not a fair comparison
Every run uses the same pairs and steps; only the number of negatives per query (7 vs 255) differs
The group-of-8 run has a larger loss, so it must learn faster
Masking changes the positive passage for each query
blocks.explain: The mask only hides other passages from each query's softmax, so data, batch, steps and positives stay fixed. That isolates the effect of the negative count, which comparing batch sizes alone cannot do, because a bigger batch also means fewer steps per epoch.

blocks.question: Your new dense model reaches nDCG@10 0.61 on a test set where BM25 reaches 0.83. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Dense retrieval does not work
nDCG@10 must be computed wrong, because dense models always beat BM25
On this data the model is not yet competitive; ship BM25 or a hybrid and keep improving the model
Use recall@100 instead, since it hides the gap
blocks.explain: The measurement says what it says: on these queries exact matching is stronger. That is a property of this data and this model, not of dense retrieval in general. Switching metrics to hide a gap only postpones the bad news.

lessons.title: Modern training: web pairs, mined negatives and distillation

blocks.md:
The recipe so far is DPR's from 2020: one labeled dataset, in-batch negatives and one BM25 negative per question. Every embedding model you are likely to download today, from the E5 and GTE families onward, adds four ingredients on top:

1. A **pre-training** stage on hundreds of millions of weak, automatically mined pairs.
2. Hard negatives mined by **the model itself**, not by BM25.
3. A filter for **false negatives**, mined passages that are actually relevant.
4. A cross-encoder **teacher** whose scores the bi-encoder learns to copy.

The query and passage prefixes you will meet in the indexing lesson also come from how these models were trained.

**Stage 1: weak pairs at web scale.** E5 (EmbEddings from bidirEctional Encoder rEpresentations; Wang and others, Microsoft, 2022) built CCPairs from text pairs that need no annotator: Reddit (post, comment), Stack Exchange (question, upvoted answer), Wikipedia (entity name plus section title, passage), scientific papers (title, abstract) and citation pairs, and (title, passage) from Common Crawl web pages and news. Heuristic filtering left about 1.3 billion pairs.

Then a **consistency-based filter**: train a model on the noisy pairs, rank each pair's passage against 1 million random passages, and keep the pair only if its passage lands in the top 2. About 270 million pairs survived. Training uses in-batch negatives only, with a batch of 32,768 and temperature 0.01 (scale 100). GTE (General Text Embeddings; Li and others, Alibaba, 2023) follows the same plan with about 800 million pairs and batches of over ten thousand.

blocks.title: E5 pre-training: batch size vs average nDCG@10 (Table 5)

scenes.caption: Average nDCG@10 times 100 over six BEIR datasets after contrastive pre-training only. With in-batch negatives as the only negatives, batch size is the number of negatives.

8k and 32k: 50.2 and 51.6. The same trend as DPR's batch ablation and the lab, at 128 times the lab's batch of 256. The E5 paper notes that hard negatives are the alternative to huge batches, but mining them for over 100 million pairs is hard engineering.

blocks.md:
**Stage 2: fine-tuning on labeled data.** E5 then trains on MS MARCO (web search questions with labeled relevant passages), NQ and NLI, with 7 mined hard negatives per example, batch 256, and a loss that mixes the contrastive loss with a KL-divergence term (a measure of how far one probability distribution is from another) pulling its softmax toward a cross-encoder teacher's. For NLI, the contradiction sentence serves as the hard negative. GTE fine-tunes with a batch of 128 and groups of 16 passages per query (1 positive, 15 hard or random negatives), noting that hard negatives make huge batches unnecessary.

Pre-training alone already mattered: E5's unsupervised base model averaged 42.9 nDCG@10 on 15 BEIR datasets against BM25's 41.7, which the paper reports as the first unsupervised model to beat BM25 there.

blocks.title: The two-stage recipe behind E5 and GTE

nodes.label:
labeled pairs
MS MARCO, NQ, NLI

scenes.caption: Stage 1 mines pairs that need no annotator and keeps only those a first model finds consistent, cutting about 1.3 billion pairs to about 270 million (E5).
Pre-training uses in-batch negatives only, so the batch is huge: 32,768 pairs for E5.
Stage 2 starts from those weights and trains on small labeled sets, each query with several hard negatives mined by a retriever.
A cross-encoder supplies soft scores to imitate and can filter false negatives. The result is the model you download.

blocks.md:
**Negatives that stay hard: ANCE.** BM25 negatives are hard *for BM25*. After some training the dense model separates them easily, their softmax probability drops toward 0, and so does their gradient, since the gradient on a negative is its probability (the in-batch lesson derived this). ANCE (Xiong and others, 2020) instead draws negatives from an approximate nearest neighbor index of the whole corpus built with a recent checkpoint of the model being trained, so the negatives are the passages the model currently confuses.

Re-encoding the corpus every step is impossible, so ANCE runs an Inferencer beside the Trainer that re-encodes the corpus with the latest checkpoint and swaps in a fresh index; for passage ranking it refreshed every 10,000 batches and sampled one negative from the top 200. The paper reports that it nearly matches BM25 followed by BERT re-ranking at about 100 times the speed.

**False negatives.** Mining from the top of a ranking has a catch: the top passages are often *relevant but unlabeled*. MS MARCO labels about 1.1 positive passages per question among 8.8 million. RocketQA (Qu and others, 2021) manually checked top-retrieved passages that were not labeled positive and found about 70% of them were actually positives or highly relevant. Train on those as negatives and the loss pushes correct answers away.

RocketQA's fix is **denoising with a cross-encoder**: score each mined candidate with a trained cross-encoder, keep it as a negative only if its score is below 0.1, and (for data augmentation) treat unlabeled passages scoring above 0.9 as positives. A manual check found these labels over 90% accurate.

blocks.prompt: Take row q2 from the in-batch lesson (cosines 0.30, 0.55 true, 0.48, 0.12) and add a mined negative n2 with cosine 0.58. A cross-encoder later gives n2 a score of 0.95: it answers the question. At scale 20, how much probability does the true passage keep, and which way does the gradient push n2?
blocks.reveal: The softmax over (p1, p2, p3, p4, n2) gives p2 only **0.325** and n2 0.592, so this row's loss jumps from 0.226 to 1.124. The gradient of this row's loss with respect to cos(q2, n2) is 20 x 0.592 = **+11.85**, the strongest push on any negative in the batch, so gradient descent lowers that cosine: it pushes a correct answer away from the question harder than it pushes away any real negative. Dropping n2 (score above 0.1) restores the original row.

blocks.title: Row q2 softmax with an unfiltered mined negative

scenes.caption: With n2 in the row, the labeled positive keeps 0.33 and the unlabeled positive n2 takes 0.59. The loss treats that as a mistake to fix.
After cross-encoder filtering n2 is gone, and the row is the familiar one: 0.80 on p2, 0.20 on the hard negative p3. Loss 0.226 instead of 1.124.

blocks.title: RocketQA ablation on MS MARCO dev (MRR@10, Table 3)

scenes.caption: MRR@10 is the average of 1/rank of the first relevant passage, cut at rank 10, times 100. Sharing negatives across GPUs (cross-batch) adds a little: 32.39 to 33.32.
Mining hard negatives from the retriever's top results without filtering makes the model worse: 26.03. Many of those negatives were answers.
The same mined negatives, filtered by a cross-encoder: 36.38, and 37.02 with the extra pseudo-labeled positives.

blocks.md: **Distillation from a cross-encoder.** A teacher gives richer labels than relevant or not. Hofstatter and others (2020) found that different ranking architectures output scores on different scales, so copying raw scores is a poor target. **Margin-MSE** asks the student only to reproduce the teacher's *margin* between a positive and a negative passage, leaving the scale free. TAS-B (2021) added **topic-aware sampling**: cluster the 400,000 MS MARCO training queries once with k-means into 2,000 clusters and fill each batch from a few clusters, so in-batch negatives share a topic and are harder. E5's KL term and GPL, in the adaptation lesson, are the same idea.

blocks.caption: M_s is the student bi-encoder's score, M_t the cross-encoder teacher's. Averaged over the batch. If the teacher scores a mined negative above the positive, the target margin is negative, which also handles false negatives softly.

blocks.md:
**Instructions and LLM embedders.** INSTRUCTOR (Su and others, 2022) embeds every text together with a task instruction such as *Represent the Wikipedia question for retrieving supporting documents:*, trained on 330 datasets each with its own instruction, so one model serves many tasks. E5-mistral (Wang and others, 2024) fine-tunes the decoder-only Mistral-7B with LoRA (low-rank adaptation: the original weights stay frozen and only small added matrices are trained) in under 1,000 steps on about 500,000 synthetic examples written by proprietary LLMs, mixed with labeled retrieval datasets. Queries get `Instruct: {task}` then `Query: {text}`; documents get no instruction, so the index does not depend on the task.

It appends an `[EOS]` (end of sequence) token and uses the last layer's vector there (**last-token pooling**), not a mean: in a decoder each token attends only to earlier ones, so only the final position has read the whole text. Prefixes and instructions were part of training, which is why leaving them out hurts. The *Asymmetric embeddings* course covers those conventions.

Before trusting a downloaded embedding model, read its card for five facts: what it was trained on, how it pools (mean, CLS or last token), which prefix or instruction each side needs, which similarity it was trained with, and its maximum input length. Each one is a silent failure if you get it wrong.

blocks.question: You mine hard negatives from your current model's top 20 for each training question and retrain. Dev recall drops, and reading the mined negatives shows many of them answer the question. What is the best fix?
options: Mine from deeper ranks only, such as positions 200 to 300, so negatives are random
Lower the scale from 20 to 1 so the false negatives matter less
Increase the batch size so the false negatives are a smaller share
Score the mined negatives with a cross-encoder and keep only those it rates clearly irrelevant
blocks.explain: This is RocketQA's false-negative problem, and its fix: a cross-encoder reads query and passage together and can tell an unlabeled answer from a near miss. Mining from deep ranks gives easy negatives with no gradient; a lower scale weakens every signal; a bigger batch still contains the same false negatives.

blocks.question: Why do BM25 negatives mined once before training lose value as dense training goes on?
options: The dense model learns to separate them, so their softmax probability, and with it their gradient, falls toward zero
BM25 scores change during training
They are deleted from the corpus
In-batch negatives replace them automatically
blocks.explain: The gradient on a negative's logit is its softmax probability. Once the model scores a fixed negative far below the positive, it contributes almost nothing. ANCE re-mines negatives from the model's own index so they stay hard.

blocks.question: E5-mistral is a decoder-only LLM. Why does it take the vector at the final [EOS] token instead of averaging all token vectors?
options: Averaging is too slow for a 7-billion-parameter model
Causal attention lets each token see only earlier tokens, so only the last position has seen the whole text
The [EOS] vector is always longer than the others
Mean pooling cannot be normalized
blocks.explain: In a decoder, early tokens never see later ones, so their vectors summarize only a prefix. The last position has attended to everything. Speed and normalization have nothing to do with it.

lessons.title: Searching a corpus: indexing, ANN and vector size

blocks.md:
With a trained bi-encoder, semantic search is two separate pipelines.

- **Offline (indexing):** split documents into passages that fit the model's input limit, encode each passage, normalize, and store the vectors in an index alongside passage ids.
- **Online (query):** encode the query with the same model, compute similarity to stored vectors, and return the top $k$.

The input limit is real: the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model card says text longer than 256 word pieces is truncated, so anything beyond that is silently ignored unless you chunk. DPR split Wikipedia into 100-word passages, giving 21,015,324 of them. How to choose the chunk size and keep context is the topic of a later lesson.

blocks.title: Indexing offline, querying online

scenes.caption: Offline: every passage goes through the encoder once. For DPR this took about 8.8 hours on 8 GPUs for 21 million passages.
Online: only the query is encoded. Its vector is compared with stored vectors and the best k ids come back.
The query must use the same model (and the same prefix or prompt convention) as the passages. Vectors from different models live in unrelated spaces.

blocks.md: A toy run, simplified to 3 dimensions so you can check it by hand. The query is *who is the bad guy in lord of the rings*, embedded and normalized to $(0.777, 0.621, 0.104)$. Five passages are already normalized in the index; each score is a dot product of unit vectors, so it is the cosine.

blocks.title: Toy corpus: cosine with the query

scenes.caption: Dot products of unit vectors. D1 shares almost no words with the query yet scores highest; D4 is unrelated and scores near 0.
Top-2 retrieval returns D1 and D2. Exact search had to score all 5 passages to know that.

blocks.md: Exact (brute-force) search scores every stored vector: $N \times d$ multiply-adds per query, where $N$ is the number of stored vectors and $d$ their dimension, because each score is one dot product of length $d$. That is fine for small corpora; the sentence-transformers docs suggest a plain implementation up to about 1 million entries. At DPR's scale it is not. DPR's encoder is BERT-base, so $d = 768$, and each number is a 4-byte float32:

blocks.caption: Compute and float32 memory for exact search over DPR's Wikipedia index.

blocks.md: **Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN)** indexes trade a little **recall** for a lot of speed. Recall here is the share of the true $k$ nearest neighbors (the ones exact search would return) that the index actually returns, not the lab's recall@k, which counts labeled relevant passages. The most widely used one is **HNSW** (hierarchical navigable small world), a layered graph of vectors that a search walks greedily toward the query. How it is built and tuned is the subject of the next course, *Vector search and ANN (HNSW)*; here only its cost matters.

DPR used FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search, Meta's open-source vector search library) with an HNSW index on CPU and reports 995 questions per second (top 100 each), against 23.7 per second per CPU thread for BM25 in Lucene. Lucene is the open-source Java search library behind Elasticsearch; it runs BM25 over an **inverted index**, a map from each word to the list of documents that contain it, so only documents with a query word are scored. The price of HNSW is paid offline: building the HNSW index took 8.5 hours, versus about 30 minutes for Lucene's inverted index.

Short queries and long passages are an **asymmetric** search task. Many models are trained with role prefixes and expect them at inference: E5 (EmbEddings from bidirEctional Encoder rEpresentations, a Microsoft model family from 2022) says every input should start with `query: ` or `passage: `. sentence-transformers exposes `encode_query` and `encode_document`, which apply a model's configured prompts. Omitting the prefix a model was trained with quietly hurts recall.

Memory scales with dimension, so smaller vectors are tempting. **Matryoshka Representation Learning**, named after Russian nesting dolls that each hold a smaller doll, trains one embedding so that its first $m$ dimensions work on their own, by adding the training loss at several nested sizes (for BERT-base, 12, 24, 48 up to 768). You can then keep only a prefix. An ordinary model was never asked to put the most useful information first, so nothing guarantees its prefixes. How much either loses depends on the model and the task, so measure it.

blocks.title: Float32 storage for 1 million vectors

scenes.caption: Each float32 dimension costs 4 bytes: 768 dims is 3,072 bytes per vector, 3.07 GB per million.
Keeping Matryoshka prefixes halves storage and per-query compute at each step. Renormalize the prefix before using dot product, since a truncated unit vector is no longer length 1.

blocks.title: Truncating 768-dim vectors on SciFact: nDCG@10 (measured)

scenes.caption: tomaarsen/mpnet-base-nli, trained with plain MultipleNegativesRankingLoss on NLI pairs, truncated and renormalized: 0.373 at 768 dims, 0.293 at 128, 0.087 at 32.

The Matryoshka twin (same base model, data and loss, plus the nested loss): 0.354, 0.253 and 0.095. On this out-of-domain retrieval set it holds up no better; both are NLI models, weak at retrieval to begin with.

blocks.md: The figure is a measurement on this Mac, not a published result. The same two models were built for the sentence-transformers Matryoshka docs, which report that on the STS benchmark (the task family they were trained for) the Matryoshka model keeps 98.37% of its score at 64 of 768 dimensions against 96.46% for the standard one. On SciFact retrieval, the standard model kept 51.5% at 64 dimensions and the Matryoshka one 54%. The *Matryoshka embeddings* course covers the training loss and when it pays off.

The other lever is the number of bits per dimension, called **embedding quantization**. **int8** (scalar) quantization maps each dimension's range to 256 levels, using a minimum and maximum per dimension computed on a calibration set: 4 times smaller than float32. **Binary** quantization keeps only the sign: 1 if the value is above 0, else 0, so 768 dimensions become 768 bits, **96 bytes**, 32 times smaller. Two binary vectors are compared by **Hamming distance**, the number of bit positions where they differ, which a CPU computes with an XOR and a population count (counting 1 bits).

The usual trick is **rescoring**: retrieve a few times more candidates than you need with the cheap codes, then re-rank just those with more precise numbers, either the float32 query against the candidates' binary codes (the Hugging Face recipe) or against float32 copies of the candidates kept on disk.

blocks.caption: DPR's 64.6 GB float32 index would fit in about 2.0 GB as binary codes.

blocks.title: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 on SciFact: nDCG@10 by encoding (measured)

scenes.caption: Baseline: 5,183 abstracts, 300 test claims, exact search with normalized float32 vectors: 0.645. Dot product on the unnormalized pooled vectors gives 0.607: this model was trained with cosine, so length is noise.
int8 with per-dimension ranges from the corpus: 0.626, 97.1% of float32 at a quarter of the memory.
Binary codes, 48 bytes each: 0.588 (91.2%). Rescoring the top 40 Hamming candidates: 0.621 with the float query against binary codes, 0.639 (99.1%) against float32 copies.

blocks.md: These are one run's results on 300 queries of one small dataset, and they measure nDCG@10 against relevance labels, which forgives near-equal swaps; the next course measures recall of exact neighbors, where binary codes lose much more. The Hugging Face embedding-quantization study ran 15 MTEB retrieval datasets: mxbai-embed-large-v1 kept 92.53% of its score with binary codes alone and 96.45% after rescoring, while e5-base-v2 kept only 74.77% with binary codes even after the same rescoring. Quantization tolerance is a property of the model, so check it on your data. The *Product quantization* and *RaBitQ and binary quantization* courses go much further.

blocks.code:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")  # 384 dims
passages = ["Sala Baker played the villain Sauron in the Lord of the Rings.",
            "Hobbits eat several meals a day."]
corpus = model.encode_document(passages, convert_to_tensor=True, normalize_embeddings=True)

query = model.encode_query("who is the bad guy in lord of the rings",
                           convert_to_tensor=True, normalize_embeddings=True)
hits = util.semantic_search(query, corpus, top_k=2, score_function=util.dot_score)
print(hits[0])  # [{'corpus_id': ..., 'score': ...}, ...]
blocks.caption: Exact search with sentence-transformers. With normalized vectors, dot_score equals cosine. Swap util.semantic_search for an ANN index (FAISS, hnswlib) at large scale.

blocks.question: You will store 10 million passages as 384-dimensional float32 vectors. Roughly how much memory do the raw vectors need?
options: 1.5 GB
3.8 GB
blocks.explain: 10,000,000 x 384 x 4 bytes = 15,360,000,000 bytes, about 15.4 GB, before any index overhead such as HNSW graph links. 3.8 GB would be 1 byte per dimension; 30.7 GB would be 768 dimensions.

blocks.question: You plan to keep the first 128 of 768 dimensions to save memory. The model card does not say whether it was trained with a Matryoshka loss. What should you do?
options: Nothing: any model keeps its quality at any prefix length
Never truncate: a non-Matryoshka model always becomes useless
Switch from cosine to dot product so truncation does not matter
Measure nDCG@10 or recall@k on your own queries at 768 and at 128 dimensions, renormalizing the prefix, and decide from the drop
blocks.explain: Prefix quality is an empirical question. Matryoshka training aims to make prefixes work; an ordinary model gives no guarantee: in the SciFact figure the standard model lost 9% at 256 dimensions but 77% at 32. Renormalize the prefix before using dot product, and decide from your own measurement.

blocks.question: With an E5 model, queries are embedded with the `query: ` prefix, but the corpus was indexed last year with no prefix at all. What should you expect?
options: Weaker retrieval, because passages were embedded without the passage prefix the model expects
No effect: the prefix only matters at training time
An error, because the vectors have different dimensions
Better retrieval, because mixing conventions adds diversity
blocks.explain: The model card instructs that each input start with query: or passage:, and the model was trained that way. The vectors still have the same dimension, so nothing crashes; quality degrades silently. Re-embed the corpus with the right prefix.

blocks.question: You store 10 million 768-dimensional embeddings as binary codes and keep float32 copies on disk for rescoring. How much RAM do the binary codes need?
options: About 7.7 GB
About 30.7 GB
About 0.96 GB
About 3.8 GB
blocks.explain: 768 bits is 96 bytes per vector; 10,000,000 x 96 bytes = 0.96 GB. int8 would be 7.68 GB and float32 30.72 GB. The float32 copies only need to be read for the few rescored candidates per query.

lessons.title: Chunking documents and adapting a model to your corpus

blocks.md:
A 10,000-token contract does not fit in all-MiniLM-L6-v2, which reads 256 word pieces and silently drops the rest. So you cut it into **chunks**, each short enough to embed, and index every chunk as its own passage. Two knobs: **chunk size** $c$ (tokens per chunk) and **overlap** $o$ (tokens shared by neighboring chunks, so a sentence cut at a boundary appears whole in one of them).

With a step of $c - o$ tokens between chunk starts, a document of $N$ tokens needs this many chunks:

blocks.tex: n = \left\lceil \frac{N - o}{c - o} \right\rceil, \qquad N = 10{,}000,\; c = 256:\quad o = 0 \Rightarrow 40, \quad o = 32 \Rightarrow 45, \quad o = 64 \Rightarrow 52

blocks.title: Chunk vectors for one 10,000-token document (chunk 256)

scenes.caption: No overlap: 40 chunks, 40 vectors to store and search.
Overlap 32 and 64: 45 and 52 vectors, 12.5% and 30% more index, and 11,408 and 13,264 tokens to encode instead of 10,000. Overlap is paid for in every index and every re-embedding.

blocks.md:
The deeper problem is **lost context**. A chunk reading *The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter* (Anthropic's example) never names the company or the quarter, so its vector cannot match a question about one company. The cheap fix is to **prepend the document title and section path** to every chunk before embedding (for example *Acme 10-Q, Q2 2023 > Results:*). When the search unit is a document, score each document by its **best chunk** (the maximum over its chunks' scores) and return each document once.

A stronger fix, Contextual Retrieval, where an LLM writes a 50 to 100 token context for each chunk, is measured in the *Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)* course. Another, [late chunking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.04701), embeds the whole document with a long-context model and mean-pools each chunk's token vectors afterward, so every chunk vector has read its surroundings.

blocks.title: Chunk, add context, embed, then map hits back to documents

scenes.caption: Offline: the contract becomes 45 overlapping chunks of 256 tokens.
Each chunk gets the contract's title and section path in front, so a clause about 'the Supplier' still says which contract it is in.
Chunks are embedded and stored with their document id.
Online: the query finds the best chunks; each document is scored by its best chunk and returned once.

blocks.question: A contract search returns exactly the right indemnity clause, but from the wrong customer's contract. The clause text never mentions the customer. Which chunking change targets this?
options: Double the chunk overlap
Prepend each chunk with its contract's title and parties (or generate a short context per chunk) before embedding
Use smaller chunks
Switch from cosine to dot product
blocks.explain: The chunk vector cannot encode a customer the text never mentions. Adding the document's identity to each chunk (title, parties, section path, or an LLM-written context) puts it into the vector. Overlap and chunk size only move boundaries; the similarity function cannot add missing information.

blocks.md:
**When the model loses on your data.** BEIR showed that dense models trained on one dataset often fall below BM25 on others. Before fixing anything, measure: collect 50 to a few hundred real queries, mark their relevant passages, and compute recall@k and nDCG@10 for BM25 and for the model.

A worked case: [SciFact](https://huggingface.co/datasets/BeIR/scifact) from BEIR matches scientific claims to the abstracts that support or refute them (5,183 abstracts, 300 test claims, and 809 training claims with labels). On this Mac, all-MiniLM-L6-v2 scored nDCG@10 0.645 on the 300 test claims and BM25 0.652: `rank_bm25`'s `BM25Okapi` with its defaults ($k_1 = 1.5$, $b = 0.75$), lowercase word tokens, no stemming or stop-word removal, title and abstract as one field. The *BM25* course gets 0.677 on the same claims by removing stop words and stemming, and BEIR reports 0.665 with Anserini (a Lucene-based research toolkit); its lesson on BM25 variants explains why BM25 numbers differ by setup. Either way, the general model is no better than keywords.

Two ways to adapt it, both with the in-batch loss you already know:

- **Labeled pairs.** If you have a few hundred (query, relevant passage) pairs, fine-tune on them with `MultipleNegativesRankingLoss`.
- **No labels: synthetic queries.** A query generator writes plausible queries for your own passages; each (generated query, passage) pair is a training example. GPL (Wang and others, 2022) uses a T5 model (Google's text-to-text transformer; a doc2query T5 is one fine-tuned on MS MARCO to write a query for a passage) to write 3 queries per passage, retrieves 50 negatives per query with an existing retriever, has a cross-encoder score the margin between positive and negative, and trains with Margin-MSE. It reports gains of up to 9.3 nDCG@10 points over the zero-shot model on six domain-specific datasets. InPars (2022) writes the queries with a large language model prompted with a few examples instead.

blocks.code:
from datasets import Dataset
from sentence_transformers import (SentenceTransformer, SentenceTransformerTrainer,
                                   SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments)
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.losses import MultipleNegativesRankingLoss
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.training_args import BatchSamplers

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
train = Dataset.from_dict({"anchor": queries, "positive": passages})  # your pairs
loss = MultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model)  # cosine, scale 20, in-batch negatives
args = SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments(
    output_dir="minilm-scifact", num_train_epochs=1,
    per_device_train_batch_size=32, learning_rate=2e-5, warmup_steps=0.1,
    batch_sampler=BatchSamplers.NO_DUPLICATES,  # no repeated text in a batch
    use_cpu=True, report_to="none")
SentenceTransformerTrainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=train, loss=loss).train()
blocks.caption: The fine-tuning call used for the figure below (sentence-transformers 6.3; older versions import the loss from sentence_transformers.losses). Then re-encode the corpus and rerun the evaluation (`InformationRetrievalEvaluator` reports recall@k and nDCG@10).

blocks.title: SciFact test nDCG@10 before and after adaptation (measured)

scenes.caption: Before: BM25 (rank_bm25 defaults, no stemming) 0.652, the general model 0.645.
One epoch on the 919 (claim, abstract) training pairs, 40 seconds on 2 CPU threads: 0.660.

No labels: one sampled query per abstract from doc2query T5-small, one epoch with in-batch negatives: 0.626 in this run, worse than doing nothing. Some generated queries are poor matches for their abstract, and nothing filters them.

blocks.md:
Why did the synthetic run lose? This is the simple query-generation recipe the GPL paper calls QGen, and GPL was designed to fix it. Its cross-encoder scores every (generated query, passage) pair, so a badly generated query gets a small target margin instead of being forced next to its passage, and a mined negative that is really relevant gets a high score instead of being pushed away. On SciFact the GPL paper reports nDCG@10 57.1 for its zero-shot MS MARCO model, 63.8 with QGen, 66.4 with GPL and 66.1 for its own BM25 run (another setup, as above).

Our starting model was already trained on over a billion pairs, including scientific titles and abstracts, so there was less to gain: in this run the labeled pairs added about 1.5 points (0.645 to 0.660). That is one run with one seed and sampled synthetic queries; on 300 claims a change this small could shrink, grow or flip on a rerun. Small gains and outright losses are normal, which is why every step here ends with a measurement.

Keep the evaluation queries out of training. Generating synthetic queries over the whole corpus, test passages included, is fair: in production you have the corpus but not the users' queries. Training on the evaluation queries, or tuning until one small dev set looks good, is not.
Synthetic queries inherit the generator's habits. Read 20 of them before training: doc2query models trained on MS MARCO write short web-search questions, which may not look like your users' queries.

blocks.question: An off-the-shelf model scores nDCG@10 0.40 on your legal corpus, BM25 scores 0.55, and you have no labeled queries. What is the most reasonable next step?
options: Generate synthetic queries for your passages, train GPL-style with cross-encoder pseudo-labels, and compare against BM25 on a small hand-labeled test set
Ship the dense model, since dense retrieval is newer
Fine-tune on MS MARCO again
Lower the similarity threshold until more passages come back
blocks.explain: Without labels, synthetic queries over your own corpus are the standard adaptation route (GPL, InPars), and the cross-encoder labels guard against bad queries. You still need a small set of real, held-out queries to tell whether it worked, and BM25 or a hybrid remains the fallback. More general-domain data does not target the domain gap.

lessons.title: Where dense retrieval fails: hybrid search and re-ranking

blocks.md: Dense retrieval is not a strict upgrade over keywords. The DPR authors observed the two fail differently: BM25 is sensitive to highly selective keywords and phrases, while DPR captures lexical variation and semantic relationships but may lack capacity for **salient phrases that appear rarely**, such as names, product codes or error strings. On SQuAD (the Stanford Question Answering Dataset), where annotators wrote questions while looking at the passage and so reused its words, BM25 beat DPR.

blocks.prompt: A support search indexes error-log passages. A user types `ERR_SSL_VERSION_INTERFERENCE`. Which retriever is more likely to put the exact matching passage first: BM25 or a general-purpose dense bi-encoder?
blocks.reveal: **BM25.** The string is a rare, highly selective token sequence; an exact match gets a large IDF (inverse document frequency) weight, because very few passages contain it. A dense model compresses the whole text into one vector, and a code it rarely saw in training may land near other SSL errors that look similar. This is why production systems often run both.

blocks.md:
The gap shows up at scale, too. **BEIR**, a benchmark for information retrieval (Thakur and others, 2021), evaluated retrievers zero-shot (no training on the target data) across 18 datasets and found BM25 a robust baseline: dense retrievers were efficient but often underperformed it out of domain, while re-ranking models (a cross-encoder rescoring the top results) and late-interaction models (which keep one vector per token and compare them at query time; the last lesson explains them) scored best at high compute cost. E5 later reported being the first model to beat BM25 on BEIR zero-shot without any labeled data.

**MTEB**, the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (8 task types, 58 datasets in its first release), found that no single embedding method dominates across all tasks. The practical rule: measure on your own queries before trusting a leaderboard.

**Hybrid search** runs BM25 and dense retrieval in parallel and merges the ranked lists. Their raw scores live on different scales, so a common merge uses ranks only: **reciprocal rank fusion** (RRF), from Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher (SIGIR 2009, the main information retrieval conference, run by the ACM Special Interest Group on Information Retrieval). A document's fused score sums $1/(k+\text{rank})$ over the lists it appears in, with $k = 60$, a value the authors fixed in a pilot study. In the formula below, $R$ is the set of ranked lists and $r(d)$ is document $d$'s rank in list $r$ (rank 1 is the top). The constant $k$ damps the bonus for top places: with $k = 60$, first place earns 1/61 and tenth place 1/70, so being found by both retrievers usually beats being first in only one.

blocks.title: Reciprocal rank fusion of two top-4 lists (scores x 1000)

scenes.caption: BM25 ranks P7 first (it contains the exact error code). The dense retriever ranks P2 first. P2 and P9 appear in both lists.
P2: 1/(60+2) + 1/(60+1) = 32.52 thousandths. P9: 1/63 + 1/63 = 31.75. Showing up in both lists beats being first in only one.
P7, first in BM25 only, gets 1/61 = 16.39 and stays in the top 3. P4 and P1 tie at 1/64 = 15.63.

blocks.md: The last stage brings back the accuracy the bi-encoder gave up. A **retrieve and re-rank** pipeline takes a modest candidate list (the sentence-transformers docs use about 100) from BM25, dense or hybrid retrieval, then scores each candidate with a **cross-encoder** that reads query and passage together. Running the expensive model on 100 passages is affordable; on 21 million it is not. DPR's own question answering system did this: its **reader**, a model that reads each retrieved passage and picks out the answer, re-scored the retrieved passages with cross-attention.

What does the re-ranker see? monoBERT (Nogueira and Cho, 2019, [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.04085)) set the pattern: feed `[CLS] query [SEP] passage [SEP]` to BERT, with the query cut to 64 tokens and the pair to 512, put one small classification layer on the `[CLS]` output, and train it with cross-entropy on relevant versus non-relevant (query, passage) pairs. The output is a relevance probability for each pair independently; sort by it. The *Cross-encoder rerankers* course covers the input packing, losses and serving in depth.

blocks.code:
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder

reranker = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2", max_length=256)
# candidates: the top 100 passages from the bi-encoder (or the RRF-fused list)
pairs = [(query, passage) for passage in candidates]
scores = reranker.predict(pairs, batch_size=32)          # one forward pass per pair
reranked = [p for _, p in sorted(zip(scores, candidates), key=lambda t: -t[0])]
blocks.caption: Re-ranking a candidate list with a MiniLM cross-encoder trained on MS MARCO.

blocks.md:
The candidate count is a latency budget: 100 candidates cost 100 forward passes. In our run on this Mac with 2 CPU threads, re-ranking 100 SciFact abstracts took about **0.78 s** per query (median of 5 queries), against about 4 ms for encoding the query and exactly scoring all 5,183 abstract vectors. A rerun while other jobs shared the CPU took about 1.6 s: CPU latency depends on load, so measure on the machine you will serve from. On a GPU the same work is far faster, but the scaling is the same: double the candidates, double the re-ranking cost.

It paid for itself here: nDCG@10 rose from 0.645 (bi-encoder alone) to 0.682 after re-ranking the top 100, and to 0.680 when re-ranking only the top 20, at a fifth of the cost.

blocks.title: A typical semantic search stack

scenes.caption: Two cheap first-stage retrievers run in parallel. BM25 catches exact rare terms; the bi-encoder catches paraphrases and synonyms.
RRF merges by rank, so the two incompatible score scales never have to be calibrated against each other.
The cross-encoder re-scores only the merged candidates, with full attention between query and passage. Simplified: real systems also add filters, caching and deduplication.

blocks.md: Each stage covers another's blind spot: BM25 for rare exact terms, the bi-encoder for meaning across different words, the cross-encoder for precise final ordering on a short list. Evaluate the whole pipeline on your own queries with the lab's metrics: recall@k for each first stage at the depth the re-ranker reads, nDCG@10 for the final list.

Misconception: a higher similarity score means a more relevant passage across queries. Cosine scores are only comparable within one query's ranking and one model. A fixed threshold like 0.7 that works for one model can be meaningless for another.

blocks.question: A dense-only search works well on natural questions but users complain that searching an exact SKU (stock keeping unit, a product code) like `KX-4471-B` returns similar-looking but wrong products. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Increase the embedding dimension from 384 to 1024
Lower the softmax temperature at query time
Switch from cosine to dot product
Add BM25 in parallel and fuse the lists with RRF
blocks.explain: Rare exact identifiers are where lexical matching is strongest and dense vectors are weakest. Hybrid retrieval keeps the dense model's paraphrase handling and adds exact-term recall. Temperature is a training-time setting; more dimensions or another similarity function do not create exact-match behavior.

blocks.question: In RRF with k = 60, document X is ranked 1st by BM25 and absent from the dense list. Document Y is ranked 3rd in both lists. Which ranks higher after fusion?
options: Y, because 2/63 is larger than 1/61
X, because a first place always wins
They tie
It depends on the raw BM25 score of X
blocks.explain: X gets 1/61, about 0.0164. Y gets 1/63 + 1/63, about 0.0317. RRF rewards agreement between retrievers, and it never looks at raw scores, so X's BM25 score is irrelevant.

blocks.question: Re-ranking costs about 0.78 s for 100 candidates on your CPU, and your latency budget for this stage is 200 ms. What is the most direct way to fit it?
options: Re-rank 1,000 candidates in one batch, which is faster per pair
Remove the bi-encoder stage
Re-rank fewer candidates (about 20), since cost grows linearly with the candidate count
Use a larger cross-encoder
blocks.explain: Each candidate is one forward pass, so 20 candidates cost about a fifth of 100. On SciFact, re-ranking the top 20 kept most of the gain (0.680 vs 0.682 nDCG@10). More candidates or a bigger model cost more, and without a first stage there is nothing to re-rank.

lessons.title: Beyond one vector: late interaction and learned sparse retrieval

blocks.md: A bi-encoder squeezes a whole passage into one vector before it has seen the query. A cross-encoder reads both together but cannot precompute anything. Two designs sit in between. BEIR found late-interaction models among its strongest zero-shot retrievers, and [SPLADE v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.10086) later reported state-of-the-art BEIR results with learned sparse vectors. This lesson places both on the map; each has its own course.

**Late interaction (ColBERT, Khattab and Zaharia, 2020).** Encode query and passage separately, as a bi-encoder does, but keep **one vector per token** (128 numbers each in the paper) instead of pooling. Passage token vectors are computed offline. At query time, each query token finds its most similar passage token, and the passage score is the sum of those maxima, called **MaxSim**. The interaction is late because it happens after both encoders have finished, and cheap because it is only dot products.

blocks.title: MaxSim: 3 query tokens against 4 passage tokens (2-d toy)

scenes.caption: Each cell is the dot product of a unit query-token vector with a unit passage-token vector (toy 2-d vectors at made-up angles).
Each query token keeps only its best match: q1 to d1 (0.985), q2 to d2 (0.996), q3 to d3 (0.985).
Score = 0.985 + 0.996 + 0.985 = 2.966. Every query token must find its own match, which a single pooled vector cannot check.

blocks.md: The price is storage. A 100-token passage in ColBERT is 100 vectors: at 128 dimensions and 2 bytes per number (ColBERT stored 16-bit values for end-to-end search) that is 25,600 bytes, against 1,536 for one 384-dim float32 vector. [ColBERTv2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.01488) (2021) cut the footprint 6 to 10 times with residual compression while improving quality. The *Late interaction (ColBERT, ColPali)* course builds MaxSim, the compression and the PLAID search engine.

**Learned sparse retrieval (SPLADE, Formal and others, 2021).** Keep the inverted index, but let a transformer choose the terms and weights. BERT's masked-language-model head already outputs a score for each of its 30,522 vocabulary terms at every token position. SPLADE applies $\log(1 + \mathrm{ReLU}(w))$ to each score (ReLU keeps only positive values; the log damps very large ones) and adds them over the token positions, giving one weight per vocabulary term (SPLADE v2 takes the maximum over positions instead) and adds a **FLOPS regularizer** to the loss that pushes most weights to exactly 0. The result is a sparse vector that can include terms the passage never uses (**expansion**), so a passage about a villain can carry weight on related words a query might use. It is served by the same inverted-index machinery as BM25. The *Learned sparse retrieval (SPLADE)* course covers it in full.

blocks.title: Four scorers on the cost and quality line

scenes.caption: Left: cheapest, everything precomputed, one vector per passage. Right: most accurate, nothing precomputed. Simplified: real costs depend on implementation.
SPLADE keeps precomputation and stores weighted terms, so it runs on an inverted index like BM25 and keeps exact term matching.
ColBERT keeps precomputation and stores token vectors, paying in index size for token-level matching at query time.

blocks.md: A rough guide: a bi-encoder plus BM25 hybrid and a cross-encoder re-ranker is the simple default. If you must stay on Lucene or Elasticsearch, learned sparse vectors fix vocabulary mismatch inside that stack. If quality out of domain matters most and you can afford the index size, late interaction. How to fuse lists (RRF versus a weighted sum of normalized scores) is covered in *Hybrid search* and *Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)*.

blocks.question: Your search runs on Elasticsearch and must stay there. Users' words often differ from the documents' (bad guy vs villain). Which approach fixes the vocabulary mismatch without new serving infrastructure?
options: ColBERT late interaction
A larger dense bi-encoder with an HNSW index
Learned sparse vectors such as SPLADE, stored as weighted terms in the inverted index
Raising BM25's k1 parameter
blocks.explain: SPLADE's output is a weight per vocabulary term, including expansion terms the document never used, which an inverted index can store and score. ColBERT and a dense bi-encoder both need a vector index. BM25 parameters only reweight words that already match.

blocks.question: Query tokens q1 and q2 against passage tokens d1, d2, d3. Dot products: q1 row (0.9, 0.2, 0.4), q2 row (0.1, 0.3, 0.6). What is the MaxSim score?
blocks.explain: Take each query token's best passage token: 0.9 for q1 and 0.6 for q2, then add them: 1.5. 2.5 would sum the whole matrix, and 0.9 is the single best cell.
